faqs.answer: Yes. Pour the 9x13 batter straight into the two rounds and the layers bake about 8 percent shallower. Check them about 5 minutes early. Scale it only when the layer height matters.
faqs.question: Can I use the same batter without scaling?

faqs.answer: Only with care. Two 8-inch rounds cover 100.5 square inches, about 9 percent less than a 9x13, so the batter sits deeper and can overflow unless the pans are a full 2 inches deep. King Arthur says to play it safe with 9-inch rounds for a new recipe.
faqs.question: Can I use two 8-inch rounds instead?

faqs.answer: No. Keep the temperature the recipe gives. The swap changes the pan shape, not the heat. Only the time moves, and at the same depth it does not move at all.
faqs.question: Do I change the oven temperature?

faqs.answer: Weigh it. Put each greased pan on the scale, tare it, and pour half the batter weight into each. A measuring cup works too: pour half the cups into each pan. Even batter means even layers, and even layers stack straight.
faqs.question: How do I split the batter evenly?

faqs.answer: Use the 9-inch rounds, never the 8-inch ones, and fill no more than two-thirds full. A high-rising batter needs the headroom, and the 9-inch rounds have the area to give it.

parts.meaning: The area of a 9x13 pan in square inches: 9 x 13.
The area of two 9-inch rounds: 2 x 63.6 square inches.

formula.text: New batter = recipe batter x 1.09. Factor = new area divided by old area = 127.2 divided by 117 = 1.09.

howToSteps.name: Work out the factor
howToSteps.text: Two 9-inch rounds cover 127.2 square inches and a 9x13 covers 117. Divide 127.2 by 117 and the factor is 1.09.

howToSteps.name: Scale every ingredient
howToSteps.text: Multiply each ingredient by 1.09, including the baking powder or soda. Leavening scales like everything else.

howToSteps.name: Split the batter evenly
howToSteps.text: Divide the scaled batter between two greased 9-inch round pans. Weigh the pans as you pour if you want even layers.

howToSteps.name: Bake as the recipe says
howToSteps.text: Same oven temperature, same bake time. Check both layers with a toothpick at the recipe time, and check 5 minutes early the first time you make the swap.

lede: A 9x13 pan covers 117 square inches and two 9-inch rounds cover 127, so the rounds hold about 9 percent more batter. Scale the recipe up by 1.09 and the layers bake at the same depth, in about the same time.

title: 9x13 to Two 9-Inch Rounds Converter
tutorial: This is the most common pan swap in baking, and King Arthur Baking works it out in full: a 9x13 pan covers 117 square inches, a 9-inch round covers 63.6, and two of them together cover 127.2. The rounds hold about 9 percent more than the rectangle, so a recipe scaled by 1.09 fills them to the same depth the sheet cake had.

The other round option is two 8-inch rounds, and King Arthur warns against it for a new recipe: two 8-inch rounds cover only 100.5 square inches, about 9 percent less than the 9x13, and the batter can overflow unless the pans are a full 2 inches deep. Two 9-inch rounds are the safe choice. The layers come out a little shorter than the sheet cake would have been, and that is a better problem than batter on the oven floor.

You can also skip the scaling and pour the 9x13 batter straight into the two rounds. The layers bake about 8 percent shallower, which is a small difference on a cake that is an inch and a half tall. Check them about 5 minutes early the first time, because thinner batter sets faster. For a celebration cake where the layers need presence, scale it. For a weeknight cake, do not bother.

A typical 9x13 cake makes about 6 cups of batter, which becomes about 6.5 cups scaled, or about 3.25 cups per round pan. Fill each round no more than two-thirds full, which is about 5.3 cups in a 9-inch round, and split the batter evenly. The easy way to split evenly is to set each pan on the scale and pour half the weight into each. Eyeballing it gives one tall layer and one short one, and the short one always ends up on top.

Bake at the same temperature and the same time as the recipe says. Same batter depth means the same bake, and both pans are 2 inches deep, so nothing about the heat changes. The only new habit is the toothpick test in both layers, not one. Ovens have hot spots, and two pans means two chances for one side to run ahead.
